mappings.note: Common name versus chemical name in a word equation. Naming convention inside the representation, so the C 1.3 competency; C 1.3-LO-1 is about a balanced symbolic equation with states, which a word equation is not.
Defines 'reactants'. Equation vocabulary under the C 1.3 competency, not the balanced-equation outcome.
Identifies MgO as the product in a given equation -- reading the representation, C 1.3.
Catalyst versus reactant. Equation vocabulary, so the competency; C 8.1-LO-1 would apply only if the question were about the symbol written over the arrow.
Names a product of zinc with dilute sulphuric acid. Product identification within the equation, C 1.3; the item does not ask for the reaction type, so not LO-1.
Total reactant mass equals total product mass -- conservation of mass stated directly, LO-2.
Counts products in CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Reading the equation, C 1.3; the decomposition label is not asked for.
Which statement about reactants and products is correct -- equation vocabulary, C 1.3.
What the substance above the arrow usually is. Interpreting notation written over the arrow is what C 8.1-LO-1 covers, unlike the plain vocabulary items around it.
The forgotten reactant in rusting is water. Corrosion conditions, LO-2, rather than generic equation vocabulary.
A substance unchanged at the end is a catalyst -- reactant/product/catalyst vocabulary, C 1.3.
A precipitate is always an insoluble solid product. Precipitation is the double-displacement clause of LO-1, so this leaves the vocabulary cluster.
What does not belong on the reactant side -- equation structure, C 1.3.
Reads the reactants out of 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Interpreting the representation, C 1.3.
A decomposition has one reactant. The discriminating knowledge is what a decomposition reaction IS, which LO-1 names, not equation vocabulary.
6 g + 16 g gives 22 g of CO2 -- conservation of mass arithmetic, LO-2.
Which species is both consumed and part of a product. Tracking species across the arrow, C 1.3.
Balance reading in a sealed flask stays constant -- conservation of mass in a closed system, LO-2.
Corrects a confusion between reactants and conditions in photosynthesis. Reactant identification, C 1.3.
Deducing that the third product must hold the lead is atom bookkeeping across the arrow, which is the conservation reasoning of LO-2.
Apparent mass loss in an open beaker because gas escapes -- the classic conservation-of-mass caveat, LO-2.
What stops a substance being a reactant -- vocabulary boundary case, C 1.3.
Two reactants, two products, one of them water points to a neutralisation, i.e. a double displacement. Reaction-type inference, LO-1.
10 g minus 6 g gives 4 g of gas -- conservation of mass arithmetic, LO-2.
Why the same substance cannot sit on both sides of a simple equation -- equation structure, C 1.3.
Iron oxide is the reduced reactant in the thermite reaction. Redox identification, LO-1, despite the item sitting in the reactants/products set.
Defines a closed system, the condition under which conservation of mass is observable on a balance -- LO-2.
12 g in, 10 g out: the shortfall must have escaped or been lost. Conservation of mass reasoning, LO-2.
Sulphate on both sides is a spectator ion, not a catalyst. A vocabulary correction about species in an equation, C 1.3.
Same reactants giving different products points to different conditions. This frame has no outcome for reaction conditions, so competency level, as with qid:84809.
Limiting reactant carries information the equation does not. A limitation of the representation, C 1.3, not the conservation reasoning of LO-2.
Mass gain in an open dish means something from the air was taken up -- conservation of mass applied to an open system, LO-2.
Burning wood only seems to break conservation of mass because the gaseous products leave. LO-2.
Doubling A while B is fixed changes nothing, because the coefficients in the balanced equation fix the ratio. Reading a balanced equation, so LO-1 rather than LO-2.

An element free on the left and combined on the right has reacted, i.e. it is a reactant now inside a product. Mapped at C 1.3 as a reactant/product tracking item; flagged as ambiguous because if the intended answer is 'has been oxidised' the item would belong at C 1.2-LO-1, and the option text is not stored.
Why physical states are written in an equation -- the 'states the physical states of the reactants and products' half of C 1.3-LO-1.
A solid vanishing with no new solid means the products are soluble. Reactant/product inference, C 1.3.
The flaw in 'any substance losing mass must be a reactant'. A reasoning check about reactant identification, C 1.3, since no mass balance is computed.
Why 'reactant' is more precise than 'ingredient' -- the vocabulary of chemical change, C 1.3.
What to check before declaring an equation wrong on a product count -- equation checking, C 1.3.
Same reactants and products but different rates: the difference lies in conditions. Reaction rate and conditions have no outcome in this frame, so competency level.
Names an equation written in formulae. Terminology for the representation, C 1.3.
Formula of water. Symbol-level recall, C 1.3, with no equation to balance.
Counts oxygen atoms in CaCO3 -- reading a formula, C 1.3.
Formula of carbon dioxide -- symbol recall, C 1.3.
What formulae let chemists do that words do not. Value of the representation, C 1.3.
Names the leading 2 in 2H2O as a coefficient. Notation terminology, C 1.3; the balancing procedure itself is not asked for.
Formula of sodium chloride -- symbol recall, C 1.3.
Reads 2Na as two sodium atoms -- coefficient interpretation, C 1.3.
Counts atoms in H2SO4 -- reading a formula, C 1.3.
Distinguishes an element's formula from a compound's -- symbol literacy, C 1.3.
Formula of quick lime (CaO) -- symbol recall, C 1.3.
Why subscripts must not be changed while balancing. A rule of the balancing procedure, so LO-1 rather than the plain notation competency.
Counts calcium atoms in 3CaCO3 -- coefficient times subscript, C 1.3.
Hydrogen gas is H2. Diatomic formula recall, C 1.3.
Translates a word equation into formulae. Representation conversion at C 1.3; the item does not turn on the coefficients.
Which formula equation represents magnesium burning. Chiefly a formula-correctness choice, so C 1.3; LO-1 is reserved here for items where balancing is the discriminator.
Calcium hydroxide as Ca(OH)2 while converting a word equation -- formula writing, C 1.3.
Counts iron atoms on the left of a given equation -- reading formulae and coefficients, C 1.3.
Formula equation for the electrolysis of water. Conversion to symbols, C 1.3.
Subscript versus coefficient in Na2SO4 -- what each position means, C 1.3.
Which formula equation matches the given word equation -- conversion correctness, C 1.3.
H2O2 is the wrong formula for water. A formula error, not a balancing error, so C 1.3.
Counts hydrogen atoms in 2Ca(OH)2 -- brackets, subscripts and coefficient together, C 1.3.
Knowing the carbonate group to write sodium carbonate -- polyatomic formula writing, C 1.3.
Correct use of brackets in a formula -- notation, C 1.3.
The main risk when converting words to formulae is writing a wrong formula. A conversion-accuracy item, C 1.3.
The sulphate group behaves as an unchanged unit. Reading polyatomic groups in an equation, C 1.3.
Objects to 'balancing' by rewriting H2O as H2O2. A balancing-procedure violation, LO-1, matching qid:705948.
Formulae make conservation of mass checkable because atoms can be counted. Straight LO-2 reasoning.
Only 2Ca + O2 -> 2CaO is balanced. The discriminator is the coefficients, so LO-1.
Why Fe2O3 is not FeO3 -- composition and valency fix the formula, C 1.3.
Correct formulae do not guarantee the reaction happens. A limitation of the representation, C 1.3.
A wrong formula survives balancing undetected. A conversion error rather than a balancing error, so C 1.3.
Different subscripts for the same element in different compounds -- valency and formula writing, C 1.3.
Counts oxygen atoms in Al2(SO4)3 -- brackets and subscripts, C 1.3.
An equation that needs no coefficients is already balanced. The judgement is about balance, so LO-1.
How a word equation relates to its formula equation -- comparing representations, C 1.3.
NaCl2 must be corrected before anything else. A formula-validity step preceding balancing, so C 1.3.
Why diatomic elements matter when writing formula equations -- formula correctness, C 1.3.
Doubled coefficients are still balanced but not the simplest ratio. A judgement about balanced forms, LO-1.
Names a skeletal equation. Terminology for the unbalanced representation, so C 1.3, not the balanced-equation outcome.
Why H2 + O2 -> H2O counts as skeletal. Recognising the unbalanced form, C 1.3.
The first step toward a balanced equation is the skeletal equation. Cited at LO-1 because the item is about the route to a balanced equation, not about skeletal equations as an end state.
In a skeletal equation the formulae are correct but the atoms are not equal -- definition, C 1.3.
Picks the skeletal equation from candidates -- recognising the unbalanced form, C 1.3.
Balancing is done by adding coefficients -- the balancing procedure, LO-1.
Skeletal equation for water decomposition. Writing the unbalanced formula equation, C 1.3.
What a skeletal equation is good for -- value of the representation, C 1.3.
Finds the unbalanced element in Al + Cl2 -> AlCl3. Atom counting in service of balancing, LO-1.
Which statement about skeletal equations is true -- definition, C 1.3.
Identifies hydrogen as the unbalanced element in Na + H2O -> NaOH + H2 -- balancing diagnosis, LO-1.
When (s) and (aq) are added to an equation. Physical states are named explicitly in C 1.3-LO-1.
Formulae must be right before balancing, or the balanced result is meaningless. A precondition of producing a correct balanced equation, LO-1.
Skeletal equation for magnesium with hydrochloric acid -- writing the unbalanced form, C 1.3.
Coefficient of Fe in the balanced Fe + O2 -> Fe2O3. Direct balancing, LO-1.
Smallest whole-number coefficients for Al + Cl2 -> AlCl3 -- balancing, LO-1.
Which equation is balanced as written. A balance judgement, LO-1.
Coefficient of NaOH after balancing -- direct balancing, LO-1.
Reducing 2,4,2,4 to the simplest whole-number set -- part of producing a properly balanced equation, LO-1.
Which element to balance last in a combustion equation -- balancing strategy, LO-1.
Coefficient of O2 in the balanced KClO3 decomposition -- direct balancing, LO-1.
Why Zn + HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2 is called skeletal. Recognising the unbalanced state, C 1.3.
Treating nitrate as a unit to balance Pb(NO3)2 -- a balancing technique, LO-1.
Clearing a half coefficient by multiplying through -- completing the balance, LO-1.
An equation that cannot be balanced reveals a wrong formula. A balancing diagnosis, LO-1.
Coefficient of H2 in the balanced ammonia synthesis -- direct balancing, LO-1.
Why skeletal equations come first in teaching -- about the representation itself, C 1.3.
Persistent failure to balance usually means a wrong formula, not an impossible reaction. Balancing diagnosis, LO-1.
Balancing changes only coefficients, never identities, so the chemistry described is untouched. A statement about the balancing operation, LO-1.
Two balanced answers differing by a common multiple -- equivalent balanced forms, LO-1.
Why free oxygen is left until last -- balancing strategy, LO-1.
Justifies treating an unchanged polyatomic group as a unit while balancing -- LO-1 technique.
A skeletal equation is not wrong, only incomplete. A judgement about the representation, so C 1.3.
Tripling every coefficient asserts the same reaction in the same ratios. Equivalent balanced forms, LO-1, as with qid:705976.
A skeletal equation records what reacts and what forms even before balancing -- value of the representation, C 1.3.
Equal atom counts obtained by altering a subscript describe a different substance, so the equation no longer represents the reaction. The deepest objection is to the balancing move itself, LO-1.
